sword_marker_records.content_osis: <div sID="gen11208" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="45" osisID="Ps.45" sID="Ps.45"/> <div eID="gen11208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11209" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11210" type="x-p"/> This psalm is an illustrious prophecy of Messiah the Prince: it is all over gospel, and points at him only, as a bridegroom espousing the church to himself and as a king ruling in it and ruling for it. It is probable that our Saviour has reference to this psalm when he compares the kingdom of heaven, more than once, to a nuptial solemnity, the solemnity of a royal nuptial, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.2">Matt. xxii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1">xxv. 1</reference>. We have no reason to think it has any reference to Solomon's marriage with Pharaoh's daughter; if I thought that it had reference to any other than the mystical marriage between Christ and his church, I would rather apply it to some of David's marriages, because he was a man of war, such a one as the bridegroom here is described to be, which Solomon was not. But I take it to be purely and only meant of Jesus Christ; of him speaks the prophet this, of him and of no other man; and to him ( <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6-Ps.45.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>) it is applied in the New Testament (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.8">Heb. i. 8</reference>), nor can it be understood of any other. The preface speaks the excellency of the song, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">ver. 1</reference>. The psalm speaks, I. Of the royal bridegroom, who is Christ. 1. The transcendent excellency of his person, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.2">ver. 2</reference>. 2. The glory of his victories, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.3-Ps.45.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. 3. The righteousness of his government, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.6-Ps.45.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. 4. The splendour of his court, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.8-Ps.45.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. II. Of the royal bride, which is the church. 1. Her consent gained, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.10-Ps.45.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. 2. The nuptials solemnized, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.12-Ps.45.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. 3. The issue of this marriage, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.16-Ps.45.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. In singing this psalm our hearts must be filled with high thoughts of Christ, with an entire submission to and satisfaction in his government, and with an earnest desire of the enlarging and perpetuating of his church in the world.

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen11210" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11209" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Nuptial Song; Glories of the Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen11211" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue <hi type="italic">is</hi> the pen of a ready writer. <hi type="super">2</hi> Thou art fairer than the children of men: grace is poured into thy lips: therefore God hath blessed thee for ever. <hi type="super">3</hi> Gird thy sword upon <hi type="italic">thy</hi> thigh, O <hi type="italic">most</hi> mighty, with thy glory and thy majesty. <hi type="super">4</hi> And in thy majesty ride prosperously because of truth and meekness <hi type="italic">and</hi> righteousness; and thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things. <hi type="super">5</hi> Thine arrows <hi type="italic">are</hi> sharp in the heart of the king's enemies; <hi type="italic">whereby</hi> the people fall under thee. <div eID="gen11211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11212" type="x-p"/> Some make <hi type="italic">Shoshannim,</hi> in the title, to signify an instrument of six strings; others take it in its primitive signification for lilies or roses, which probably were strewed, with other flowers, at nuptial solemnities; and then it is easily applicable to Christ who calls himself the <hi type="italic">rose of Sharon and the lily of the valleys,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.2.1">Cant. ii. 1</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">a song of loves,</hi> concerning the holy love that is between Christ and his church. It is a <hi type="italic">song of the well-beloved,</hi> the virgins, the companions of the bride (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">v. 14</reference>), prepared to be sung by them. The virgin-company that attend the Lamb on Mount Zion are said to <hi type="italic">sing a new song,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.3-Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen11212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11213" type="x-p"/> I. The preface (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">v. 1</reference>) speaks, 1. The dignity of the subject. It is <hi type="italic">a good matter,</hi> and it is a pity that such a moving art as poetry should every be employed about a bad matter. It is <hi type="italic">touching the King,</hi> King Jesus, and his kingdom and government. Note, Those that speak of Christ speak of a good matter, no subject so noble, so copious, so fruitful, so profitable, and so well-becoming us; it is a shame that this good matter is not more the matter of our discourse. 2. The excellency of the management. This song was a confession with the mouth of faith in the heart concerning Christ and his church. (1.) The matter was well digested, as it well deserved: <hi type="italic">My heart is inditing it,</hi> which perhaps is meant of that Spirit of prophecy that dictated the psalm to David, that Spirit of Christ which was in the prophets, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>. But it is applicable to his devout meditations and affections in his heart, out of the abundance of which his mouth spoke. Things concerning Christ ought to be thought of by us with all possible seriousness, with fixedness of thought and a fire of holy love, especially when we are to speak of those things. We then speak best of Christ and divine things when we speak from the heart that which has warmed and affected us; and we should never be rash in speaking of the things of Christ, but weigh well beforehand what we have to say, lest we speak amiss. See <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Eccl. v. 2</reference>. (2.) It was well expressed: <hi type="italic">I will speak of the things which I have made.</hi> He would express himself, [1.] With all possible clearness, as one that did himself understand and was affected with the things he spoke of. Not, "I will speak the things I have heard from others," that is speaking by rote; but, "the things which I have myself studied." Note, What God has wrought in our souls, as well as what he has wrought for them, we must declare to others, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. [2.] With all possible cheerfulness, freedom, and fluency: "<hi type="italic">My tongue is</hi> as <hi type="italic">the pen of a ready writer,</hi> guided by my heart in every word as the pen is by the hand." We call the prophets the <hi type="italic">penmen</hi> of scripture, whereas really they were but the pen. The tongue of the most subtle disputant, and the most eloquent orator, is but the pen with which God writes what he pleases. Why should we quarrel with the pen if bitter things be written against us, or idolize the pen if it write in our favour? David not only spoke what he thought of Christ, but wrote it, that it might spread the further and last the longer. His tongue was as the pen of a ready writer, that lets nothing slip. When the heart is inditing a good matter it is a pity but the tongue should be as <hi type="italic">the pen of a ready writer,</hi> to leave it upon record. <div eID="gen11213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11214" type="x-p"/> II. In these verses the Lord Jesus is represented, <div eID="gen11214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11215" type="x-p"/> 1. As most beautiful and amiable in himself. It is a marriage-song; and therefore the transcendent excellencies of Christ are represented by the beauty of the royal bridegroom (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art fairer than the children of men,</hi> than any of them. He proposed (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.1">v. 1</reference>) to speak of the King, but immediately directs his speech to him. Those that have an admiration and affection for Christ love to go to him and tell him so. Thus we must profess our faith, that we see his beauty, and our love, that we are pleased with it: <hi type="italic">Thou are fair,</hi> thou art <hi type="italic">fairer than the children of men.</hi> Note, Jesus Christ is in himself, and in the eyes of all believers, more amiable and lovely than the children of men. The beauties of the Lord Jesus, as God, as Mediator, far surpass those of human nature in general and those which the most amiable and excellent of the children of men are endowed with; there is more in Christ to engage our love than there is or can be in any creature. Our beloved is more than another beloved. The beauties of this lower world, and its charms, are in danger of drawing away our hearts from Christ, and therefore we are concerned to understand how much he excels them all, and how much more worthy he is of our love. <div eID="gen11215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11216" type="x-p"/> 2. As the great favourite of heaven. He is <hi type="italic">fairer than the children of men,</hi> for God has done more for him than for any of the children of men, and all his kindness to the children of men is for his sake, and passes through his hands, through his mouth. (1.) He has grace, and he has it for us; <hi type="italic">Grace is poured into thy lips.</hi> By his word, his promise, his gospel, the good-will of God is made known to us and the good work of God is begun and carried on in us. He received all grace from God, all the endowments that were requisite to qualify him for his work and office as Mediator, that from his fulness we might receive, <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>. It was not only poured into his heart, for his own strength and encouragement, but poured into his lips, that by the words of his mouth in general, and the kisses of his mouth to particular believers, he might communicate both holiness and comfort. From this grace poured into his lips proceeded those gracious words which all admired, <reference osisRef="Luke.4.22">Luke iv. 22</reference>. The gospel of grace is poured into his lips; for it <hi type="italic">began to be spoken by the Lord,</hi> and from him we receive it. He has the words of eternal life. <hi type="italic">The spirit of prophecy is put into thy lips;</hi> so the Chaldee. (2.) He has the blessing, and he has it for us. "Therefore, because thou art the great trustee of divine grace for the use and benefit of the children of men, <hi type="italic">therefore God has blessed thee for ever,</hi> has made thee an everlasting blessing, so as that in thee all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." Where God gives his grace he will give his blessing. We are blessed with spiritual blessings in Christ Jesus, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Eph. i. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen11216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11217" type="x-p"/> 3. As victorious over all his enemies. The royal bridegroom is a man of war, and his nuptials do not excuse him from the field of battle (as was allowed by the law, <reference osisRef="Deut.24.5">Deut. xxiv. 5</reference>); nay, they bring him to the field of battle, for he is to rescue his spouse by dint of sword out of her captivity, to conquer her, and to conquer for her, and then to marry her. Now we have here, <div eID="gen11217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11218" type="x-p"/> (1.) His preparations for war (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O Most Mighty!</hi> The word of God is the sword of the Spirit. By the promises of that word, and the grace contained in those promises, souls are made willing to submit to Jesus Christ and become his loyal subjects; by the threatenings of that word, and the judgments executed according to them, those that stand it out against Christ will, in due time, be brought down and ruined. By the gospel of Christ many Jews and Gentiles were converted, and, at length, the Jewish nation was destroyed, according to the predictions of it, for their implacable enmity to it; and paganism was quite abolished. The sword here girt on Christ's thigh is the same which is said to <hi type="italic">proceed out of his mouth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.19.15">Rev. xix. 15</reference>. When the gospel was sent fort to be preached to all nations, then our Redeemer girded his sword upon his thigh. <div eID="gen11218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11219" type="x-p"/> (2.) His expedition to this holy war: He goes forth <hi type="italic">with his glory and his majesty,</hi> as a great king takes the field with abundance of pomp and magnificence—his sword, his glory, and majesty. In his gospel he appears transcendently great and excellent, bright and blessed, in the honour and majesty which the Father had laid upon him. Christ, both in his person and in his gospel, had nothing of external glory or majesty, nothing to charm men (for he had no form nor comeliness), nothing to awe men, for he <hi type="italic">took upon him the form of a servant;</hi> it was all spiritual glory, spiritual majesty. There is so much grace, and therefore glory, in that word, <hi type="italic">He that believes shall be saved,</hi> so much terror, and therefore majesty, in that word, <hi type="italic">He that believes shall not be damned,</hi> that we may well say, in the chariot of that gospel, which these words are the sum of, the Redeemer rides forth in glory and majesty. <hi type="italic">In thy majesty ride prosperously,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.4">v. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Prosper thou; ride thou.</hi> This speaks the promise of his Father, that he should prosper according to <hi type="italic">the good pleasure of the Lord,</hi> that he should <hi type="italic">divide the spoil with the strong,</hi> in recompence of his sufferings. Those cannot but prosper to whom God says, Prosper, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10-Isa.52.12">Isa. lii. 10-12</reference>. And it denotes the good wishes of his friends, praying that he may prosper in the conversion of souls to him, and the destruction of all the powers of darkness that rebel against him. "<hi type="italic">Thy kingdom come;</hi> Go on and prosper." <div eID="gen11219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11220" type="x-p"/> (3.) The glorious cause in which he is engaged—<hi type="italic">because of truth, and meekness, and righteousness,</hi> which were, in a manner, sunk and lost among men, and which Christ came to retrieve and rescue. [1.] The gospel itself is <hi type="italic">truth, meekness, and righteousness;</hi> it commands by the power of truth and righteousness; for Christianity has these, incontestably, on its side, and yet it is to be promoted by meekness and gentleness, <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.12-1Cor.4.13">1 Cor. iv. 12, 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2 Tim. ii. 25</reference>. [2.] Christ appears in it in his <hi type="italic">truth, meekness,</hi> and <hi type="italic">righteousness,</hi> and these are his glory and majesty, and because of these he shall prosper. Men are brought to believe on him because he is true, to learn of him because he is meek, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Matt. xi. 29</reference> (the gentleness of Christ is of mighty force, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.1">2 Cor. x. 1</reference>), and to submit to him because he is righteous and rules with equity. [3.] The gospel, as far as it prevails with men, sets up in their hearts <hi type="italic">truth, meekness, and righteousness,</hi> rectifies their mistakes by the light of truth, controls their passions by the power of meekness, and governs their hearts and lives by the laws of righteousness. Christ came, by setting up his kingdom among men, to restore those glories to a degenerate world, and to maintain the cause of those just and rightful rulers under him that by error, malice, and iniquity, had been deposed. <div eID="gen11220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11221" type="x-p"/> (4.) The success of his expedition: "<hi type="italic">Thy right hand shall teach thee terrible things;</hi> thou shalt experience a wonderful divine power going along with thy gospel, to make it victorious, and the effects of it will be terrible things." [1.] In order to the conversion and reduction of souls to him, there are terrible things to be done; the heart must be pricked, conscience must be startled, and the terrors of the Lord must make way for his consolations. This is done by the right hand of Christ. The Comforter shall continue, <reference osisRef="John.16.8">John xvi. 8</reference>. [2.] In the conquest of the gates of hell and its supporters, in the destruction of Judaism and Paganism, terrible things will be done, which will make <hi type="italic">men's hearts fail them for fear</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.26">Luke xxi. 26</reference>) and great men and chief captains call to the <hi type="italic">rocks and mountains to fall on them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.15">Rev. vi. 15</reference>. The next verse describes these terrible things (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy arrows are sharp in the heart of the king's enemies. First,</hi> Those that were by nature enemies are thus wounded, in order to their being subdued and reconciled. Convictions are like the arrows of the bow, which are sharp in the heart on which they fasten, and bring people to fall under Christ, in subjection to his laws and government. Those that thus fall on this stone shall by broken, <reference osisRef="Matt.21.44">Matt. xxi. 44</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those that persist in their enmity are thus wounded, in order to their being ruined. The arrows of God's terrors are sharp in their hearts, whereby they shall fall under him, so as to be made his footstool, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>. Those that would not have him to reign over them shall be brought forth and slain before him (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.27">Luke xix. 27</reference>); those that would not submit to his golden sceptre shall be broken to pieces by his iron rod.

Some make Shoshannim, in the title, to signify an instrument of six strings; others take it in its primitive signification for lilies or roses, which probably were strewed, with other flowers, at nuptial solemnities; and then it is easily applicable to Christ who calls himself the rose of Sharon and the lily of the valleys, Cant. ii. 1 . It is a song of loves, concerning the holy love that is between Christ and his church. It is a song of the well-beloved, the virgins, the companions of the bride ( v. 14 ), prepared to be sung by them. The virgin-company that attend the Lamb on Mount Zion are said to sing a new song, Rev. xiv. 3, 4 . I. The preface ( v. 1 ) speaks, 1. The dignity of the subject. It is a good matter, and it is a pity that such a moving art as poetry should every be employed about a bad matter. It is touching the King, King Jesus, and his kingdom and government. Note, Those that speak of Christ speak of a good matter, no subject so noble, so copious, so fruitful, so profitable, and so well-becoming us; it is a shame that this good matter is not more the matter of our discourse. 2. The excellency of the management. This song was a confession with the mouth of faith in the heart concerning Christ and his church. (1.) The matter was well digested, as it well deserved: My heart is inditing it, which perhaps is meant of that Spirit of prophecy that dictated the psalm to David, that Spirit of Christ which was in the prophets, 1 Pet. i. 11 . But it is applicable to his devout meditations and affections in his heart, out of the abundance of which his mouth spoke. Things concerning Christ ought to be thought of by us with all possible seriousness, with fixedness of thought and a fire of holy love, especially when we are to speak of those things. We then speak best of Christ and divine things when we speak from the heart that which has warmed and affected us; and we should never be rash in speaking of the things of Christ, but weigh well beforehand what we have to say, lest we speak amiss. See Eccl. v. 2 . (2.) It was well expressed: I will speak of the things which I have made. He would express himself, [1.] With all possible clearness, as one that did himself understand and was affected with the things he spoke of. Not, "I will speak the things I have heard from others," that is speaking by rote; but, "the things which I have myself studied." Note, What God has wrought in our souls, as well as what he has wrought for them, we must declare to others, Ps. lxvi. 16 . [2.] With all possible cheerfulness, freedom, and fluency: " My tongue is as the pen of a ready writer, guided by my heart in every word as the pen is by the hand." We call the prophets the penmen of scripture, whereas really they were but the pen. The tongue of the most subtle disputant, and the most eloquent orator, is but the pen with which God writes what he pleases. Why should we quarrel with the pen if bitter things be written against us, or idolize the pen if it write in our favour? David not only spoke what he thought of Christ, but wrote it, that it might spread the further and last the longer. His tongue was as the pen of a ready writer, that lets nothing slip. When the heart is inditing a good matter it is a pity but the tongue should be as the pen of a ready writer, to leave it upon record. II. In these verses the Lord Jesus is represented, 1. As most beautiful and amiable in himself. It is a marriage-song; and therefore the transcendent excellencies of Christ are represented by the beauty of the royal bridegroom ( v. 2 ): Thou art fairer than the children of men, than any of them. He proposed ( v. 1 ) to speak of the King, but immediately directs his speech to him. Those that have an admiration and affection for Christ love to go to him and tell him so. Thus we must profess our faith, that we see his beauty, and our love, that we are pleased with it: Thou are fair, thou art fairer than the children of men. Note, Jesus Christ is in himself, and in the eyes of all believers, more amiable and lovely than the children of men. The beauties of the Lord Jesus, as God, as Mediator, far surpass those of human nature in general and those which the most amiable and excellent of the children of men are endowed with; there is more in Christ to engage our love than there is or can be in any creature. Our beloved is more than another beloved. The beauties of this lower world, and its charms, are in danger of drawing away our hearts from Christ, and therefore we are concerned to understand how much he excels them all, and how much more worthy he is of our love. 2. As the great favourite of heaven. He is fairer than the children of men, for God has done more for him than for any of the children of men, and all his kindness to the children of men is for his sake, and passes through his hands, through his mouth. (1.) He has grace, and he has it for us; Grace is poured into thy lips. By his word, his promise, his gospel, the good-will of God is made known to us and the good work of God is begun and carried on in us. He received all grace from God, all the endowments that were requisite to qualify him for his work and office as Mediator, that from his fulness we might receive, John i. 16 . It was not only poured into his heart, for his own strength and encouragement, but poured into his lips, that by the words of his mouth in general, and the kisses of his mouth to particular believers, he might communicate both holiness and comfort. From this grace poured into his lips proceeded those gracious words which all admired, Luke iv. 22 . The gospel of grace is poured into his lips; for it began to be spoken by the Lord, and from him we receive it. He has the words of eternal life. The spirit of prophecy is put into thy lips; so the Chaldee. (2.) He has the blessing, and he has it for us. "Therefore, because thou art the great trustee of divine grace for the use and benefit of the children of men, therefore God has blessed thee for ever, has made thee an everlasting blessing, so as that in thee all the nations of the earth shall be blessed." Where God gives his grace he will give his blessing. We are blessed with spiritual blessings in Christ Jesus, Eph. i. 3 . 3. As victorious over all his enemies. The royal bridegroom is a man of war, and his nuptials do not excuse him from the field of battle (as was allowed by the law, Deut. xxiv. 5 ); nay, they bring him to the field of battle, for he is to rescue his spouse by dint of sword out of her captivity, to conquer her, and to conquer for her, and then to marry her. Now we have here, (1.) His preparations for war ( v. 3 ): Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, O Most Mighty! The word of God is the sword of the Spirit. By the promises of that word, and the grace contained in those promises, souls are made willing to submit to Jesus Christ and become his loyal subjects; by the threatenings of that word, and the judgments executed according to them, those that stand it out against Christ will, in due time, be brought down and ruined. By the gospel of Christ many Jews and Gentiles were converted, and, at length, the Jewish nation was destroyed, according to the predictions of it, for their implacable enmity to it; and paganism was quite abolished. Those cannot but prosper to whom God says, Prosper, Isa. lii. 10-12 . And it denotes the good wishes of his friends, praying that he may prosper in the conversion of souls to him, and the destruction of all the powers of darkness that rebel against him. " Thy kingdom come; Go on and prosper." (3.) The glorious cause in which he is engaged— because of truth, and meekness, and righteousness, which were, in a manner, sunk and lost among men, and which Christ came to retrieve and rescue. He here fills his throne with judgment. It is God the Father that says to the Son here, <hi type="italic">Thy throne, O God! is forever and ever,</hi> as appears <reference osisRef="Heb.1.8-Heb.1.9">Heb. i. 8, 9</reference>, where this is quoted to prove that he is God and has a <hi type="italic">more excellent name than the angels.</hi> The Mediator is God, else he neither would have been able to do the Mediator's work nor fit to wear the Mediator's crown. The eternity of it; it is <hi type="italic">for ever and ever.</hi> It shall continue on earth throughout all the ages of time, in despite of all the opposition of the gates of hell; and in the blessed fruits and consequences of it it shall last as long as the days of heaven, and run parallel with the line of eternity itself. Perhaps even then the glory of the Redeemer, and the blessedness of the redeemed, shall be in a continual infinite progression; for it is promised that not only of his government, but of <hi type="italic">the increase of his government and peace, there shall be no end</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.7">Isa. ix. 7</reference>); even when the kingdom shall be <hi type="italic">delivered up to God even the Father</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>) the throne of the Redeemer will continue. 2. The equity of it: <hi type="italic">The sceptre of thy kingdom,</hi> the administration of thy government, <hi type="italic">is right,</hi> exactly according to the eternal counsel and will of God, which is the eternal rule and reason of good and evil. Whatever Christ does he does none of his subjects any wrong, but gives redress to those that do suffer wrong: <hi type="italic">He loves righteousness, and hates wickedness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">v. 7</reference>. He himself loves to do righteousness, and hates to do wickedness; and he loves those that do righteousness, and hates those that do wickedness. By the holiness of his life, the merit of his death, and the great design of his gospel, he has made it to appear that he loves righteousness (for by his example, his satisfaction, and his precepts, he has brought in an everlasting righteousness), and that he hates wickedness, for never did God's hatred of sin appear so conspicuously as it did in the sufferings of Christ. 3. The establishment and elevation of it: <hi type="italic">Therefore God, even thy God</hi> (Christ, as Mediator, called God <hi type="italic">his God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>, as commissioned by him, and the head of those that are taken into covenant with him), <hi type="italic">has anointed thee with the oil of gladness. Therefore,</hi> that is, (1.) "In order to this righteous government of thine, God has given thee his Spirit, that divine unction, to qualify thee for thy undertaking," <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">Isa. lxi. 1</reference>. 1. <hi type="italic">The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because he has anointed me.</hi> What God called him to he fitted him for, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Isa. xi. 2</reference>. The Spirit is called <hi type="italic">the oil of gladness</hi> because of the delight wherewith Christ was filled in carrying on his undertaking. He was anointed with the Spirit <hi type="italic">above all his fellows,</hi> above all those that were anointed, whether priests or kings. (2.) "In recompence of what thou has done and suffered for the advancement of righteousness and the destruction of sin God has anointed thee with the oil of gladness, has brought thee to all the honours and all the joys of thy exalted state." <hi type="italic">Because he humbled himself, God has highly exalted him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.8-Phil.2.9">Phil. ii. 8, 9</reference>. His anointing him denotes the power and glory to which he is exalted; he is invested in all the dignities and authorities of the Messiah. And his anointing him with the oil of gladness denotes <hi type="italic">the joy that was set before him</hi> (so his exaltation is expressed, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb. xii. 2</reference>) both in the light of his <hi type="italic">Father's countenance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.28">Acts ii. 28</reference>) and in the success of his undertaking, which he shall <hi type="italic">see, and be satisfied,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 11</reference>. This he is anointed with <hi type="italic">above all his fellows,</hi> above all believers, who are his brethren, and who partake of the anointing—they by measure, he without measure. But the apostle brings it to prove his pre-eminence above the angels, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.4">Heb. i. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.9">9</reference>. The salvation of sinners is the joy of angels (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.10">Luke xv. 10</reference>), but much more of the Son. <div eID="gen11224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11225" type="x-p"/> II. He keeps his court with splendour and magnificence. 1. His robes of state, wherein he appears, are taken notice of, not for their pomp, which might strike an awe upon the spectator, but their pleasantness and the gratefulness of the odours with which they were perfumed (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">They smell of myrrh, aloes, and cassia</hi> (the <hi type="italic">oil of gladness</hi> with which he and his garments were anointed): these were some of the ingredients of the holy anointing oil which God appointed, the like to which was not to be made up for any common use (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.23-Exod.30.24">Exod. xxx. 23, 24</reference>), which was typical of the unction of the Spirit which Christ, the great high priest of our profession, received, and to which therefore there seems here to be a reference. His royal palaces are said to be <hi type="italic">ivory</hi> ones, such as were then reckoned most magnificent. We read of an ivory house that Ahab made, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.22.39">1 Kings xxii. 39</reference>. The mansions of light above are the <hi type="italic">ivory palaces,</hi> whence all the joys both of Christ and believers come, and where they will be for ever in perfection; for by them he is made glad, and all that are his with him; for they shall enter into the joy of their Lord. 3. The beauties of his court shine very brightly. In public appearances at court, when the pomp of it is shown, nothing is supposed to contribute so much to it as the splendour of the ladies, which is alluded to here, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">v. 9</reference>. (1.) Particular believers are here compared to the ladies at court, richly dressed in honour of the sovereign: <hi type="italic">Kings' daughters are among thy honourable women,</hi> whose looks, and mien, and ornaments, we may suppose, from the height of their extraction, to excel all others. All true believers are born from above; they are the children of the King of kings. These attend the throne of the Lord Jesus daily with their prayers and praises, which is really their honour, and he is pleased to reckon it his. The numbering of kings' daughters among his honourable women, or maids of honour, intimates that the kings whose daughters they were should be tributaries to him and dependents on him, and would therefore think it a preferment to their daughters to attend him. (2.) The church in general, constituted of these particular believers, is here compared to the queen herself—the queen-consort, whom, by an everlasting covenant, he hath betrothed to himself. She stands <hi type="italic">at his right hand,</hi> near to him, and receives honour from him, in the richest array, <hi type="italic">in gold of Ophir,</hi> in robes woven with golden thread or with a gold chain and other ornaments of gold. This is <hi type="italic">the bride, the Lamb's wife,</hi> whose graces, which are her ornaments, are compared to <hi type="italic">fine linen, clean and white</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Rev. xix. 8</reference>), for their purity, here to <hi type="italic">gold of Ophir,</hi> for their costliness; for, as we owe our redemption, so we owe our adorning, not to corruptible things, but to <hi type="italic">the precious blood of the Son of God.</hi>

entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen11225" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Glory of the Church.</title> <div sID="gen11226" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Hearken, O daughter, and consider, and incline thine ear; forget also thine own people, and thy father's house; <hi type="super">11</hi> So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty: for he <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy Lord; and worship thou him. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the daughter of Tyre <hi type="italic">shall be there</hi> with a gift; <hi type="italic">even</hi> the rich among the people shall intreat thy favour. <hi type="super">13</hi> The king's daughter <hi type="italic">is</hi> all glorious within: her clothing <hi type="italic">is</hi> of wrought gold. <hi type="super">14</hi> She shall be brought unto the king in raiment of needlework: the virgins her companions that follow her shall be brought unto thee. <hi type="super">15</hi> With gladness and rejoicing shall they be brought: they shall enter into the king's palace. <hi type="super">16</hi> Instead of thy fathers shall be thy children, whom thou mayest make princes in all the earth. <hi type="super">17</hi> I will make thy name to be remembered in all generations: therefore shall the people praise thee for ever and ever. <div eID="gen11226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11227" type="x-p"/> This latter part of the psalm is addressed to the royal bride, standing on the right hand of the royal bridegroom. God, who said to the Son, <hi type="italic">Thy throne is for ever and ever,</hi> says this to the church, which, upon the account of her espousals to the Son, he here calls his <hi type="italic">daughter.</hi> <div eID="gen11227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11228" type="x-p"/> I. He tells her of the duties expected from her, which ought to be considered by all those that come into relation to the Lord Jesus: "<hi type="italic">Hearken,</hi> therefore, <hi type="italic">and consider</hi> this, <hi type="italic">and incline thy ear,</hi> that is, submit to those conditions of thy espousals, and bring thy will to comply with them." This is the method of profiting by the word of God. <hi type="italic">He that has ears, let him hear,</hi> let him hearken diligently; he that hearkens, let him consider and weigh it duly; he that considers, let him incline and yield to the force of what is laid before him. And what is it that is here required? <div eID="gen11228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11229" type="x-p"/> 1. She must renounce all others. <div eID="gen11229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11230" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is the law of her espousals: "<hi type="italic">Forget thy own people and thy father's house,</hi> according to the law of marriage. Retain not the affection thou hast had for them, nor covet to return to them again; banish all such remembrance (not only of thy people that were dear to thee, but of thy father's house that were dearer) as may incline thee to look back, as Lot's wife to Sodom." When Abraham, in obedience to God's call, had quitted his native soil, he was not so much as <hi type="italic">mindful of the country whence he came out.</hi> This shows, [1.] How necessary it was for those who were converted from Judaism or paganism to the faith of Christ wholly to cast out the old leaven, and not to bring into their Christian profession either the Jewish ceremonies or the heathen idolatries, for these would make such a mongrel religion in Christianity as the Samaritans had. [2.] How necessary it is for us all, when we give up our names to Jesus Christ, to hate father and mother, and all that is dear to us in this world, in comparison, that is, to love them less than Christ and his honour, and our interest in him, <reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Luke xiv. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen11230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11231" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is good encouragement given to the royal bride thus entirely to break off from her former alliances: <hi type="italic">So shall the king greatly desire thy beauty,</hi> which intimates that the mixing of her old rites and customs, whether Jewish or Gentile, with her religion, would blemish her beauty and would hazard her interest in the affections of the royal bridegroom, but that, if she entirely conformed to his will, he would delight in her. The beauty of holiness, both on the church and on particular believers, is in the sight of Christ of great price and very amiable. Where that is he says, <hi type="italic">This is my rest for ever; here will I dwell, for I have desired it.</hi> Among the golden candlesticks he walks with pleasure, <reference osisRef="Rev.2.1">Rev. ii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen11231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11232" type="x-p"/> 2. She must reverence him, must love, honour, and obey him: <hi type="italic">He is thy Lord, and worship thou him.</hi> The church is to be subject to Christ as the wife to the husband (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.24">Eph. v. 24</reference>), to call him <hi type="italic">Lord,</hi> as Sarah called Abraham, and to obey him (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.6">1 Pet. iii. 6</reference>), and so not only to submit to his government, but to give him divine honours. We must worship him as God, and our Lord; for this is the will of God, that <hi type="italic">all men should honour the Son even as they honour the Father;</hi> nay, in so doing it is reckoned that they honour the Father. Those that help to support the honour of Christ on earth shall in heaven see his glory, and share in it, and be for ever praising him. In the believing hope of our everlasting happiness in the other world let us always keep up the remembrance of Christ, as our only way thither, in our generation; and, in assurance of the perpetuating of the kingdom of the Redeemer in the world, let us transmit the remembrance of him to succeeding generations, that his name may endure for ever and be as the days of heaven.

It is probable that our Saviour has reference to this psalm when he compares the kingdom of heaven, more than once, to a nuptial solemnity, the solemnity of a royal nuptial, Matt. xxii. 2 ; xxv. 1 . We have no reason to think it has any reference to Solomon's marriage with Pharaoh's daughter; if I thought that it had reference to any other than the mystical marriage between Christ and his church, I would rather apply it to some of David's marriages, because he was a man of war, such a one as the bridegroom here is described to be, which Solomon was not. But I take it to be purely and only meant of Jesus Christ; of him speaks the prophet this, of him and of no other man; and to him ( ver. 6, 7 ) it is applied in the New Testament ( Heb. i. 8 ), nor can it be understood of any other. The preface speaks the excellency of the song, ver. 1 . The psalm speaks, I. Of the royal bridegroom, who is Christ. 1. The transcendent excellency of his person, ver. 2 . 2. The glory of his victories, ver. 3-5 . 3. The righteousness of his government, ver. 6, 7 . 4. The splendour of his court, ver. 8, 9 . II. Of the royal bride, which is the church. 1. Her consent gained, ver. 10, 11 . 2. The nuptials solemnized, ver. 12-15 . 3. The issue of this marriage, ver. 16, 17 . In singing this psalm our hearts must be filled with high thoughts of Christ, with an entire submission to and satisfaction in his government, and with an earnest desire of the enlarging and perpetuating of his church in the world.
